Kaur v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

2 Nov 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1651Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
The applicant sought leave to appeal from a decision of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Div 2) refusing an extension of time to review a Registrar's summary dismissal of her judicial review application. The underlying Tribunal decision affirmed refusal of a Regional Employer Nomination (subclass 187) visa because her employer's nomination had not been approved. Hill J dismissed the leave application and fixed costs at $5,000.
Key holding

Where a subclass 187 visa criterion requires an approved employer nomination, and the nomination has never been approved and can never now be approved, refusal is the only decision open and leave to appeal will be refused because remittal would be futile.

In this case, as explained, the Tribunal made the only decision that was open to it to make: the Applicant's employer nomination was not approved at the time of the Tribunal's decision, and therefore the 187 visa could not be granted. Further, the Tribunal has refused an application to review the refusal of that employer nomination.

Wheatland and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration)

30 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2525Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Wheatland’s Class TY Subclass 444 Special Category visa after his fraud convictions produced a substantial criminal record and he failed the character test. It accepted the fraud offending was “serious” under Direction 110 but not “very serious,” and set aside the non-revocation decision, substituting a decision to revoke the cancellation.

Cheng v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

30 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1631Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
The Federal Court dismissed Ms Cheng’s judicial review application challenging an Administrative Review Tribunal decision that affirmed non-revocation of her visa cancellation under s 501(3A). The Court rejected claims that the Tribunal committed jurisdictional error in its treatment of her drug history, rehabilitation evidence, community expectations and legal consequences. The application was dismissed with costs.
Key holding

HZCP prevents a Tribunal from going behind facts that support the conviction and sentence, but it does not bar consideration of historical facts that did not support the sentence.

So, even if the finding by the sentencing judge is to be construed as a finding that Ms Cheng had never been a drug user, it was only the finding as at the time of offending that supported the sentencing. The principles in HZCP did not concern factual findings that did not support the sentence that was made.

Singh v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

30 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1638Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a dismissal of judicial review of a Tribunal decision refusing a partner visa because the appellant did not satisfy Schedule 3 criterion 3001 and the Tribunal was not satisfied there were compelling reasons to waive it. The appellant raised numerous grounds, including new points and late AI-prepared grounds, but the Court refused leave for most new points and dismissed the appeal.
Key holding

In migration appeals, leave to raise a new point not taken below may be granted where it clearly has merit and there is no real prejudice to the respondent, but is generally refused where there is no adequate explanation and the point is of doubtful merit.

Specifically in relation to migration cases, where an adverse decision may have various serious consequences for an appellant, the Court may grant leave to raise such a new point that was not taken below if the point clearly has merit and there is no real prejudice to the respondent in permitting it to be agitated.

Arias v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

30 Oct 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2026] FedCFamC2G 1903Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
This case concerned two out-of-time judicial review applications by a Colombian citizen challenging ART decisions affirming the cancellation of his Bridging C (Subclass 030) visa and the refusal of his Partner (Temporary) (Subclass 820) visa. The Court refused both extensions of time because the proposed grounds had no reasonable prospects of success and ordered costs in each matter.
Key holding

Under s 477(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), an extension of time should be refused where the proposed grounds of judicial review have no prospects of success.

Where there are no prospects of the applicant's grounds of review succeeding, an extension is to be refused.

Palmer and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration)

29 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2519Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
Michael Allan Palmer, a New Zealand citizen who had lived in Australia since infancy, sought review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his Class TY Subclass 444 Special Category (Temporary) visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal affirmed the non-revocation decision, finding he did not pass the character test and that there was no other reason to revoke the cancellation.
Key holding

Under Direction 110 para 7(2), the Tribunal gave the protection of the Australian community greater weight than other primary considerations because of the seriousness of the offending and the risk of reoffending.

The Tribunal has decided to afford this primary consideration greater weight than the other primary considerations under paragraph 7(2) of the Direction given the nature and seriousness of the Applicant's offending, and the Applicant's risk to the Australian community should he reoffend.

Naberezhnov and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration)

28 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2522Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
The Tribunal reviewed the delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Naberezhnov’s Class BB Subclass 155 visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Although he did not pass the character test, the Tribunal was satisfied there was another reason to revoke the cancellation and set aside the review decision.
Key holding

Where an applicant does not pass the character test, the Tribunal must determine whether there is another reason to revoke the mandatory cancellation under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), applying Direction No 110.

It follows that the only issue for determination is whether I am satisfied that there is another reason why the visa cancellation decision should be revoked.

Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority

28 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1615Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.
Key holding

Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

Busson and Chief Executive Officer, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS)

27 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2503Tribunal review
The Tribunal reviewed an NDIS access refusal for an applicant with chronic spinal pain, psychosocial impairments and ADHD. It accepted permanent physical impairments but found the psychosocial/ADHD impairments not permanent because treatment had recently changed and remained under review, and it found no qualifying substantially reduced functional capacity or early intervention benefit. The decision under review was affirmed under s 105(a) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth).
Key holding

For permanence under s 24(1)(b) and r 5.6, continuing treatment does not itself prevent a finding; the issue is whether further treatment or review is needed to show the impairment is enduring.

The question is therefore not whether every possible treatment has been exhausted, nor whether treatment continues. It is whether further treatment or review is required to demonstrate the permanence of the particular impairment.

Simmons and Tax Practitioners Board (Taxation and business)

27 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2502Tribunal reviewTax
An 86-year-old chartered accountant and long-standing registered tax agent sought review of the Tax Practitioners Board's decision to terminate his registration and bar him from reapplying for three years. The Board found he made false declarations in his 2022 and 2025 renewal applications, had not completed CPE since 2014, had systemic late lodgement of his own and his company's returns, disclosed client information to offshore contractors without authorisation, and allowed an unregistered company to provide tax agent services.
Key holding

Before declaring in a renewal application that answers are true and correct, a tax agent must take steps to verify their accuracy; a false answer given without appropriate checks breaches the Code's honesty and integrity obligation.

The duty to act with honesty and integrity requires careful assessment of the matters raised in the renewal process. If unsure about the answer, then an answer should not be given.

ZKDP and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration)

Yang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship)

27 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2501Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal to approve Australian citizenship by descent under s 17(1A) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), because the delegate was not satisfied the applicant had an Australian citizen parent at the time of her birth under s 16(2)(a). The Tribunal affirmed the refusal after finding the documentary evidence unreliable or insufficient and the claimed parent-child relationship with Mr Yang not established at birth.
Key holding

For the purposes of s 16(2)(a) of the Citizenship Act, a claimed parent-child relationship, whether biological or non-biological, must be shown to have existed at the time of the child’s birth and cannot be established by a later relationship.

Hence, in considering whether the Applicant may be the non-biological child of an Australian citizen parent, the relationship must have existed at the time of the birth of the child. The relationship cannot be developed at a later stage.

Key holding

Under s 19(2) of the ART Act, delay is a relevant but not automatically determinative factor in the multifactorial assessment of reasonableness, and a very long delay may set a high bar for an applicant.

The nature of the multifactorial inquiry is such that there will invariably be cases where the gravity of one factor (eg delay) will be so great and will set the bar for the applicant so high that, as a general proposition, it will be unlikely that the factual matrix will be one where it is "reasonable in all the circumstances" for the Tribunal to exercise its discretion under s 19(2).

Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

27 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1602Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationCharacter testMigration
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. The third ground concerning asserted Torres Strait ties failed.
Key holding

The limits of the primary considerations in Direction 110 do not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by a visa cancellation review applicant.

Thai and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship)

26 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2518Tribunal reviewMigration
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal of Australian citizenship by conferral because the applicant had been an unlawful non-citizen for 29 days during the four years before his application. The Tribunal found he did not satisfy the general residence requirement and no exemption or administrative-error discretion applied. The refusal was affirmed.
Key holding

A person cannot satisfy the general residence requirement in s 22(1)(b) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth) if they were present in Australia as an unlawful non-citizen at any time during the four years immediately before the citizenship application, unless a statutory exemption or discretion applies.

I am of the view that the Applicant cannot overcome his failure to meet the general residence requirement. This is because of an obvious failure to satisfy s 22(1)(b) of the Act.

MFRVY and CEO, NATIONAL DISABILITY INSURANCE AGENCY (NDIS)

26 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2504Tribunal reviewMigration
MFRVY concerned Tribunal review of an NDIS Statement of Participant Supports for a 12-year-old with autism-related impairments. The Tribunal applied the amended s 34 criteria, including the new direct-impairment requirement, and approved increased support coordination but did not approve the additional disputed support-worker and transport funding. The decision was set aside and remitted with specific directions.
Key holding

Section 34(1)(aa) of the NDIS Act, as amended by the 2026 Amending Act, requires that funded supports address only needs arising directly from an accepted impairment, displacing Eastham’s causal or contributory approach.

The 2026 Amending Act means this no longer applies and that supports to be funded under the NDIS must now address only a need arising directly from an accepted impairment (my emphasis).

Before: Leeming JA; Ball JA; Price AJA at [1] Decision: 1. The Tribunal is directed, pur
The NSW Court of Appeal dealt with a notice of motion by the Secretary seeking variations to earlier orders remitting disciplinary proceedings and costs to NCAT. The Court refused to vary the remitter because its scope was already clear, but directed NCAT under cl 29(8)(d) that it may determine the remitted costs of the appeal without being satisfied of special circumstances. Key holding

The Court of Appeal may, under cl 29(8)(d) of Sch 5 to the NCAT Act, direct NCAT to determine remitted costs without requiring special circumstances under s 60.

The power extends to authorising the Tribunal to depart from the rule in s 60 (which rule is explicitly displaced in a number of places in the Act: see Schedule 3 cll 12 and 13 and Schedule 5 cll 23 and 26, and Civil and Administrative Tribunal Rules 2014, rr 38 and 38A).

Bhardwaj and Commissioner of Taxation (Taxation)

23 Oct 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2482Tribunal reviewCorporations
The Tribunal reviewed a self-represented taxpayer’s objection decision concerning deductions for work-related car, travel, clothing, self-education, other expenses, gifts and tax affairs, plus interest on money borrowed to buy shares. It disallowed most deductions and held the interest was capital and not deductible, but allowed $67,500 as the third element of the cost base of the shares. The objection decision was varied accordingly.
Key holding

Interest under a bona fide loan is incurred in the income year it becomes due and payable and may be included in the third element of the cost base even if not paid.

The Tribunal expressed its view that, consistent with the established principle as expressed in Federal Commissioner of Taxation v James Flood Pty Ltd [1953] HCA 65; (1953) 88 CLR 492, the interest became due and payable in the 2020 - 21 income year and, accordingly, the balance of $67,500 was, if shown to be deductable or otherwise allowable in the cost base, deductible or allowable in its entirety in the 2020 - 21 income year.

Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

23 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1589Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.
Key holding

Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

Testart v Testart (No 3)

22 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1558Tribunal reviewVisa nominationEmployment & workplace
This matter concerned Ms Testart’s attempt to vacate a stay and reinstate her Fair Work proceeding after the trustee of her bankrupt estate elected under s 60(2) Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth) to discontinue it; the sequestration order was later set aside. The Federal Court treated her application as one to set aside the discontinuance but refused relief because she did not challenge the trustee’s decision within the 60-day period in r 90-80 and gave no sufficient explanation for the delay.
Key holding

A party seeking a late procedural indulgence must satisfactorily explain the delay, and the Court will weigh prejudice and the administration of justice in deciding whether to grant it.

Accordingly, a party who seeks a late procedural indulgence must provide a satisfactory explanation for the delay, and the Court is entitled to consider not only prejudice to the opposing party but also the impact upon the administration of justice and the efficient use of judicial resources: Aon Risk Services Australia Ltd v Australian National University (2009) 239 CLR 175; UBS AG v Tyne (2018) 265 CLR 77.

This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). Le v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

25 Sep 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2026] FedCFamC2G 1864Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
This was a judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Partner (Temporary) (Class UK) visa because the applicant was not satisfied to be the spouse under s 5F of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) and reg 1.15A of the Migration Regulations 1994 (Cth). The applicant challenged adverse credibility/reliability findings as arbitrary, irrational and lacking evidentiary foundation, and alleged a failure to consider evidence with an active intellectual process. The Court dismissed the application with costs.
Key holding

Adverse credibility or reliability findings are reviewable for jurisdictional error, but a court will not substitute its own view on the merits where the Tribunal’s findings were reasonably open and its reasoning was not irrational, illogical or otherwise legally unreasonable.

The question is whether the particular reliance on inconsistencies, the findings of implausibility, any assumptions made, or the treatment of corroborative evidence reveal reasoning that is irrational, illogical or otherwise legally unreasonable. If the Tribunal's findings were reasonably open to it, the function of the Court in this matter is not to form its own view on the merits about the reliability of the evidence, including the significance of the inconsistencies, nor the weight to be given to such matters.

EDP25 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship

25 Sep 2026Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2026] FedCFamC2G 1863Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
EDP25 sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of her protection visa. She claimed to be a lesbian who would face harm in Malaysia, but the Tribunal rejected her sexual-orientation claim based on inconsistencies and implausibility. The Court found no jurisdictional error and dismissed the application.
Key holding

Where a tribunal rejects the core factual premise of a protection claim, it need not separately consider whether harm would arise from that rejected premise.

It is well established that a claim may not be expressly considered because it has been subsumed by a finding of greater generality or because the underlying core factual premise has been rejected (see Applicant WAEE v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural and Indigenous Affairs (2003) 236 FCR 593 at [47]). Once the Tribunal rejected the applicant's claim in respect of her sexual orientation, no risk could sensibly be considered to arise from that.

Ozolins v State of Queensland (Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support)

25 Sep 2026QIRC[2026] QIRC 305Tribunal reviewVisa nominationEmployment & workplace
Before: O'Neill IC
Ms Ozolins was a fixed-term temporary Senior Assessor with the Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support whose employment had been extended repeatedly. On review under s 115 of the Public Sector Act 2022 (Qld), the Department refused to convert her to permanent because funding beyond 30 June 2027 was uncertain. The QIRC allowed her appeal, finding the refusal was not fair and reasonable and converting her employment to permanent.
Key holding

Where an employee otherwise meets the conversion criteria, uncertainty about future funding will not ordinarily constitute a genuine operational requirement preventing conversion if the ongoing need and likelihood of future funding are established.

This was a review of a refusal of a Visitor (Class FA) Subclass 600 visa on genuine temporary entrant grounds under cl 600.211. The Tribunal reconsidered, on remittal from the Federal Circuit and Family Court, a delegate's decision to cancel Cyber Computer Recycling & Disposal Pty Ltd's approval as a standard business sponsor under s 140M of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). While the Tribunal has found that there existed adverse information in that the applicant failed to declare the information relating to Jomol Shibu and ITS IT Australia in the manner required, it would be counterintuitive for the Tribunal to now make a decision that it was not reasonable to disregard that information in circumstances where the Department effectively has disregarded the same information in approving the applicant's most recent standard business sponsorship approval.

Egerton and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security)

28 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2345Tribunal review
This matter concerned an age pensioner whose rate of payment was reduced after Centrelink treated about half of a terminal illness insurance payout, transferred to his former wife and carer, as a disposal of assets. The Tribunal had to decide whether the care she had provided was “consideration” for the transfer, meaning it should not be assessed under the gifting/disposal rules. The Tribunal held that the transfer was gratuitous and affirmed the decision under review.
Key holding

A transfer to a carer is not for consideration merely because it fairly compensates past care; absent a binding promise, exchange, or legal or equitable obligation to pay, the transfer is gratuitous and assessable under the disposal-of-assets rules.

I accept Mr Egerton's view that the payment was fair compensation for Mrs Egerton's care and labour, but absent any legal or equitable obligation to pay for that care and labour, the payment was gratuitous.

Yerburgh and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security)

22 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2291Tribunal reviewVisa nominationProperty
In Yerburgh and Secretary, Department of Social Services [2026] ARTA 2291, the Tribunal reviewed a decision reducing Mrs Yerburgh’s age pension by assessing notional income from a farm treated as an unrealisable asset. The Tribunal set aside the decision and remitted the rate for reassessment from 11 October 2024 on the basis that the relevant income amount was her actual annual ordinary income from the farm, not a commercial lease value.
Key holding

Where an unrealisable farm is already being worked commercially to full capacity, the amount reasonably expected from a purely commercial application under s 1130(5)(b) is the actual income from current operations, and the s 1130(5) notional rate is the lesser of that amount and 2.5% of the farm's value.

However, having heard from Mrs Yerburgh, the Tribunal is satisfied that the farm is currently being operated commercially to its full capacity. As such, the Tribunal finds that what Mrs Yerburgh could reasonably be expected to obtain from a purely commercial application of the farm is the income that is actually being generated from its current operations, not some alternative higher commercial lease figure as adopted by Centrelink.

Rodham and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security)

16 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2346Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationEmployment & workplace
Mr Rodham's jobseeker payment was cancelled after he failed to enter a Job Plan (employment pathway plan) by 22 July 2025, notwithstanding that he had lodged a Centrelink medical certificate on 24 June 2025 certifying incapacity until 24 September 2025. Centrelink did not record the temporary incapacity exemption until 19 July 2025 and conceded it could locate no record of having told him he had to enter a Job Plan within 28 days. The Tribunal set aside the cancellation and substituted a decision that payment remained payable.
Key holding

Where a claimant holds a medical certificate exempting them from mutual obligation requirements for the relevant period, and Centrelink's delay in recording that exemption (combined with a failure to notify the plan requirement) puts compliance beyond the claimant's control, the claimant is not required to satisfy the employment pathway plan requirements and payment remains payable.

The Tribunal is satisfied that these are circumstances which are beyond the person's control which made it unreasonable to expect Mr Rodham to comply with the employment pathway plan requirements in accordance with subsection 40L(2) of the Administration Act, such that a determination is in effect that Mr Rodham was not required to satisfy the employment pathway requirements for the period 24 June 2025 to 24 September 2025.

Kirby and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security)

The Tribunal reviewed a Centrelink decision raising a $4,109.18 newstart allowance debt against Mr Kirby for 30 November 2018 to 1 April 2019 due to undeclared employment income. Any recalculated overpayment remains a Commonwealth debt and recovery was not waived.
Key holding

Where pre-7 December 2020 Division 3 work income is reviewed and neither the entitlement period in which it was earned nor the payroll period can be identified, it must be assessed under s 1117D(9) in the entitlement period in which it was received.

This means that the third approach in subsection 1117D(9) must be used so that [Mr Kirby's] wages are to be assessed on each day of the newstart allowance entitlement period in which he received the income.

Littlepage and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security)

14 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2447Tribunal reviewVisa cancellation
This case concerned a child care subsidy debt of $1,171.64 for 2018-19 raised after the family’s actual adjusted taxable income exceeded the income estimate used for payments. The Tribunal affirmed the debt and found no basis for write-off or waiver, despite the income increase occurring late in the year after childcare had ceased and Centrelink’s significant delay in pursuing the debt.
Key holding

Child care subsidy entitlement is determined by annual income for the year in which each CCS fortnight starts, and the Tribunal has no discretion to substitute a point-in-time income figure.

I see the point, but the legislation operates to determine entitlement based on annual - not point in time - income for the year in which each 'CCS fortnight' starts (see, particularly, clause 3 of Schedule 2 to the Act). There is no discretion to look behind that method and substitute some income figure other than annual income for a particular period.

Harvey and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security)

13 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2293Tribunal review
In Harvey and Secretary, Department of Social Services [2026] ARTA 2293, Mrs Harvey sought review of a Centrelink decision raising and recovering an FTB debt of $4,106.55 for 2023–24 after her actual adjusted taxable income exceeded her estimates. The Tribunal found the overpayment was correctly calculated under s 71 and that neither administrative-error waiver nor discretionary waiver applied. It affirmed the decision under review.
Key holding

For discretionary waiver under s 101, special circumstances require the individual circumstances to be outside the usual or ordinary course; mere inadvertence, financial hardship or administrative delay will not suffice.

Special circumstances' is not a term defined in the legislation. For waiver on the basis of special circumstances to apply, it is necessary to examine the individual circumstances of the case and find something about a person's circumstances to take their situation out of the usual or ordinary course (for example, Dranichnikov v Centrelink [2003] FCAFC 133).

Lind and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security)

In Lind and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security) [2026] ARTA 2296, Ms Lind sought review of Centrelink’s suspension of her jobseeker payment while she travelled to [Country 1] to visit her mother after a hip fracture. The Tribunal considered whether her absence was for an approved portability reason, specifically an acute family crisis. The Tribunal affirmed the suspension because her mother was not critically ill or hospitalised at the time Ms Lind departed Australia.
Key holding

Jobseeker payment is portable for an acute family crisis only where the absence is for visiting a family member who is critically ill, meaning their condition is severe or grave or there is a crisis in the condition.

Although the Act does not define what constitutes being critically ill, the case law indicates that "critically" must be given its ordinary meaning and that a person's condition must be severe or grave or that there must be a crisis in the condition - see, for example, Al Umari and Secretary, DFaCS [2003] AATA 431.

Ludlam and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security)

The Tribunal reviewed Centrelink’s rejection of Ms Ludlam’s jobseeker payment claim because her combined assets exceeded the applicable limit. Key holding

Key holding

Economic hardship or lack of support does not amount to persecution or significant harm unless an entity in the receiving country would cause that harm.

Each of the verbal phrases contained in the categories of harm which form the definition of 'significant harm' contemplate that there is an entity in the country concerned which would cause that harm; that is, 'will be arbitrarily deprived of', 'will be carried out on', and 'will be subjected to'. Because there is no entity which would seek to cause any of those categories of harm to the Applicant, he does not meet the statutory criterion for complementary protection.

eSafety Commissioner v Baumgarten [2026] FCAFC 12 (18 February 2026)

18 Feb 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 12Migration: court challengeTribunal review
The Full Court dismissed the eSafety Commissioner’s appeal from the Administrative Review Tribunal, which had found it had jurisdiction to review a “complaint alert” sent to X about Ms Baumgarten’s post. The Tribunal treated the alert as a decision in fact to give a removal notice under s 88 of the Online Safety Act 2021 (Cth), even though the Commissioner said it was informal and not legally effective. The Full Court upheld that approach and the appeal was dismissed with no costs.
Key holding

For Tribunal review jurisdiction, a decision in fact to give a notice is reviewable as a s 88 removal notice if its objective features amount to such a notice, regardless of the decision-maker’s subjective intention or the notice’s legal effectiveness.

All that is required is that a decision to give a notice of some kind was made, and that, having regard to its objective features, the notice that was given amounts, as a matter of fact, to a removal notice as described in s 88(1).

Spaleta v Secretary, Department of Social Services [2026] FCAFC 5 (11 February 2026)

11 Feb 2026Federal Court of Australia (Full Court)[2026] FCAFC 5Tribunal reviewVisa nomination
This was a Full Court appeal about a disability support pension claim. The appellant challenged the AAT’s finding that her conditions were not fully treated or stabilised, so she could not get 20 impairment points under s 94(1)(b) of the Social Security Act 1991 (Cth). The Full Court allowed the appeal, holding that “reasonable treatment” under the Impairment Tables Determination requires consideration of whether treatment is affordable to the claimant, and remitted the matter.
Key holding

In assessing whether treatment is “reasonable treatment” under s 6(7) of the Impairment Tables Determination, “reasonable cost” requires consideration of whether the treatment is reasonably affordable to the claimant in their circumstances, not merely whether the cost is objectively reasonable in the market.

A question arises as to whether the reference to "reasonable cost" in s 6(7)(b) is to the objective reasonableness of the cost of the treatment, or to the different question whether the treatment is reasonably affordable to a claimant in the position of the person concerned. In our view, the latter is the better construction having regard to the context and purpose of the provision.

September 2025 (1)

2114521 (Refugee)

16 Sep 2025Administrative Review Tribunal[2025] ARTA 3466Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s refusal of a subclass 866 protection visa to a Chinese national who claimed persecution arising from a family shop/land dispute involving local government, a developer and his father’s petitioning. At hearing, the applicant contradicted those written claims, said he did not fear harm on return to China, and explained he wished to stay in Australia for work and family financial reasons. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

An applicant for a protection visa bears the responsibility to establish all statutory elements by sufficient evidence, and the Tribunal is not required to make the applicant’s case.

It remains for the applicant to satisfy the Tribunal that all of the statutory elements are established. A decision-maker is not required to make the applicant's case for him or her.

2002567 (Refugee)

11 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4218Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Don Smyth
This was an AATA review of a delegate’s refusal of a protection visa to an applicant who claimed South African citizenship but was born and lived in Zimbabwe. He claimed fear in South Africa and/or Zimbabwe as a gay, mixed-race/“coloured” man, a political opponent of Zanu-PF, and because of economic conditions and crime. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

For complementary protection, a real risk is not established where the risk is one faced by the population generally and not personally by the applicant.

Under s 36(2B)(c) of the Act there is taken not to be a real risk that an applicant will suffer significant harm if the Tribunal is satisfied that the real risk is one faced by the population generally and is not faced by the applicant personally.

2016849 (Refugee)

11 Oct 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4209Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Lilly Mojsin
This was an Administrative Review Tribunal (Migration & Refugee Division) review of a delegate’s refusal to grant protection visas to Chinese applicants who claimed harm from loan sharks, debt collectors, gangdom and police in China. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal because the applicants consented to a decision on the papers and the Tribunal was not satisfied their claims were made out or that they faced a real chance or real risk of harm on return to China.
Key holding

A protection visa applicant bears the onus of establishing all statutory elements; mere assertions of feared persecution or significant harm are insufficient unless they satisfy the Tribunal that a well-founded fear or real risk exists.

The mere fact that a person claims fear of persecution for a particular reason does not establish either the genuineness of the asserted fear or that it is "well-founded" or that it is for the reason claimed. Similarly, that the applicant claims to face a real risk of significant harm does not establish that such a risk exists, or that the harm feared amounts to "significant harm".

Key holding

General economic conditions causing disadvantage do not amount to persecution unless the discrimination is for a Convention reason.

Financial hardship arising from general economic conditions or re-establishment after return does not amount to significant harm under s 36(2A) because it lacks intentional infliction of pain or suffering.

Such financial hardship, while it may cause stress and anxiety, is not the result of intentionally inflicted pain or suffering by any person or group.

Key holding

A protection visa applicant bears the responsibility to provide sufficient evidence to establish each statutory element; merely claiming a fear or risk does not establish the claim.

The mere fact that a person claims fear of persecution for a particular reason does not establish either the genuineness of the asserted fear or that it is 'well-founded' or that it is for the reason claimed. Similarly, that an applicant claims to face a real risk of significant harm does not establish that such a risk exists, or that the harm feared amounts to 'significant harm'.

Once the Tribunal has validly reviewed a reviewable decision, that decision ceases to be reviewable and the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to review the same delegate decision again.

2115044 (Refugee)

24 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3976Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Sue Zelinka
The applicant, a Macedonian citizen, sought review of a refusal of a protection visa based on feared harm from family and an alleged criminal gang after his secret marriage to his first cousin became known. The Tribunal accepted the marriage and societal stigma but found no real chance of serious harm, given the divorce, his father’s reconciliation, his second marriage, and that “Komiti” was a football supporters’ club. It affirmed the refusal.
Key holding

A particular social group claim cannot succeed where the asserted group is not cognisable because its defining marriage is unlawful in the receiving country, or where the group is defined only by a shared fear of persecution or family harm.

The Tribunal rejects this formulation noting that there is no such group because first cousins, by law, cannot marry in Macedonia and therefore there cannot be a large, cognisable group of them. Any other variation of particular social group involving victims of harm at family hands is also rejected because a particular social group cannot be constituted by persons bound only by fear of persecution.

Cai (Migration)

23 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3835Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Paul Windsor
Mr Cai applied for a Visitor (Class FA) subclass 600 visa in the Tourist stream. The delegate refused the visa because it was not satisfied he genuinely intended to stay temporarily in Australia under cl 600.211. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding his long continuous stay and unsupported medical claims indicated he was using the visitor visa to establish de facto residence.
Key holding

To satisfy cl 600.211, the applicant must positively satisfy the Tribunal of a genuine intention to stay temporarily for the visa purpose; a long continuous stay without a credible departure timeframe or supporting medical evidence can show the visitor visa is being used for de facto residence.

Given the applicant has been in Australia continuously since January 2020 and could not give any time-frame within which he might feel well enough to depart Australia, the Tribunal considers the applicant is seeking to use the subclass 600 Visitor visa to establish de facto residence in Australia. Consequently, the Tribunal is not satisfied that the visa applicant genuinely intends to stay temporarily in Australia for the purpose for which the visa would be granted.

An applicant for protection must specify all particulars of the claim and provide sufficient evidence to establish it; the Tribunal is not required to specify or establish the claim and need not accept allegations uncritically.

The Tribunal does not have any responsibility or obligation to specify, or assist in specifying, any particulars of the claim, or to establish or assist in establishing the claim.

Key holding

Where an applicant for a Subclass 188 Investor visa provides no evidence of the required net business and personal assets for the relevant period, the Tribunal cannot be satisfied that cl 188.245 is met and will affirm the refusal.

For a Subclass 115 visa, because cl 115.221 requires the applicant to continue to satisfy cl 115.211, a failure to meet reg 1.15(1)(c) at the time of application cannot be cured by later circumstances.

Before: T. Quinn

A student visa holder’s failure to maintain enrolment in a full-time registered course breaches condition 8202 and enlivens the s 116(1)(b) cancellation ground, after which cancellation is a discretionary decision.

The issue in this case is whether the applicant, as the holder of a student visa, has breached condition 8202 of the Regulations. If so, the ground for cancellation is made out and the issue then becomes whether the visa should be cancelled pursuant to section 116(1) of the Act.

Hughes and Minister for Immigration, Citizenship, and Multicultural Affairs (Migration)

4 Sep 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3158Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewCharacter testMigration
Michael Hughes, a 58-year-old New Zealand/United Kingdom citizen, had his subclass 189 visa mandatorily cancelled after being convicted of indecent dealing with a child under 13 and sentenced to 20 months’ imprisonment. He sought review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke that cancellation under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal affirmed the non-revocation decision, applying Direction no. 110 and refusing to go behind the conviction and sentence.
Key holding

In a s 501CA review, the Tribunal cannot go behind the essential facts of the conviction and sentence that founded the mandatory cancellation, and an applicant bears a heavy onus to challenge those facts.

In those circumstances, it is not open to the Tribunal to go behind the essential facts of that conviction and sentence. Moreover, the Applicant has not discharged what would otherwise be his "heavy onus" to challenge the facts upon which the conviction and sentence are necessarily based as set out above.

Key holding

A protection visa cannot be granted unless the applicant is in Australia, because s 36(2) requires the applicant to be a non-citizen in Australia.

Before: Christine Kannis
The Tribunal reviewed cancellation of a Subclass 500 (Student) visa because the first applicant was not enrolled in a full-time registered course from 20 January 2022 to 5 January 2023. It affirmed cancellation, finding breach of condition 8202(2)(a) and no sufficient discretionary reasons against cancellation. It also held it had no jurisdiction over the secondary applicants, whose visas were automatically cancelled under s 140(1).
Key holding

Once a breach of condition 8202 grounds cancellation under s 116(1)(b) and cancellation is not mandatory under s 116(3), the Tribunal must proceed to exercise the discretion whether to cancel.

For these reasons, the Tribunal is satisfied that the ground for cancellation in s 116(1)(b) exists. As that ground does not require mandatory cancellation under s 116(3), the Tribunal must proceed to consider whether to exercise its discretion to cancel the visa.

An applicant over 18 at the time of application cannot satisfy the r 1.03 step-child definition for a Subclass 802 visa where reliance is placed on being the child of a former spouse/de facto partner, even if the sponsor holds a Family Law Act sole parental responsibility order.

He was 18 years at the time of application, therefore he does not meet the requirements of the definition of step child in subparagraph (b) of the definition in r.1.03, despite the Family Law Act 1975 court order dated 24 February 2020 which gave the sponsor sole parental responsibility for him.

2411479 (Refugee)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3799Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Peter Katsambanis
The Tribunal found it had no jurisdiction to review a refusal of a protection visa because the review application was lodged late. The delegate refused the visa on 6 April 2024, but the applicant did not lodge her review until 10 May 2024, outside the 28-day period.
Key holding

For a protection visa review where the applicant is not in immigration detention, the application must be lodged within 28 days starting on the day of notification; if lodged late, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction.

As the applicant was not in immigration detention on the day the applicant was notified of the decision, an application for review of the decision had to be made within 28 days, commencing on that day: reg 4.31(2) of the Migration Regulations 1994 (Cth) (the Regulations).

2018087 (Refugee)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3612Tribunal reviewMigration
Before: Michael Brereton
The Tribunal confirmed the dismissal of a protection visa review application after the applicant failed to attend the scheduled hearing and did not seek reinstatement within 14 days. The decision under review was therefore taken to be affirmed. This was a procedural non-appearance outcome, not a merits assessment.
Key holding

Where a review applicant fails to attend a Tribunal hearing and does not apply for reinstatement within the statutory 14-day period, the Tribunal must confirm the dismissal and the underlying decision is taken to be affirmed.

As the applicant did not apply for reinstatement of the application within the 14 days period, the Tribunal must confirm the decision to dismiss the application. In these circumstances, the decision under review is taken to be affirmed.

Barik (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3417Tribunal reviewVisa nominationVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Sheridan Aster
The Tribunal considered an application to review a refusal to grant a Training (Class GF) Subclass 407 visa. Because the associated nomination had been refused and the applicant was not nominated by an approved sponsor at the time of the review application, the Tribunal found the visa refusal was not a reviewable decision. The application was therefore dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Key holding

A refusal of a Training (Subclass 407) visa is reviewable only if, at the time of the review application, the applicant has an approved sponsor nomination or has a pending review of the nomination refusal.

A decision to refuse a Training visa is reviewable if the applicant made the visa application while in the migration zone and the applicant is nominated by an approved sponsor at the time the application for review of the visa refusal is made or an application for review of a decision not to approve the nomination has been made but at the time the application for review of the visa refusal is made, review of the decision is pending.

Gowing Advisory Chartered Accountants (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3416Tribunal reviewVisa nominationMigration
Before: Rosa Gagliardi

The applicant had paid part of the fee but declined to pay the balance and sought a refund.
Key holding

A migration review application is not valid, and the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction, where the prescribed fee has not been paid within the prescribed period or any applicable reasonable period after a hardship-reduction determination.

The Tribunal considers the applicant has been given a reasonable period to pay the fee since being notified of the authorised officer's decision; however, the fee has not been paid. The application for review is therefore not a valid application and the Tribunal has no jurisdiction in this matter.

Jiang (Migration)

28 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 3198Tribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Before: Tania Flood
The Tribunal affirmed refusal of Ms Jiang’s Visitor (Class FA) Subclass 600 visa because she applied after her substantive visa expired. It found the late application resulted from forgetfulness and inadequate reminders, not factors beyond her control under Schedule 3 criterion 3004(c). The applicant was also offshore at the time of decision, so cl 600.411 was not met.
Key holding

Under criterion 3004(c), whether the applicant ceased to hold a substantive visa because of factors beyond their control is assessed subjectively and practically, and forgetfulness or failure to take available compliance measures will not ordinarily qualify.

The test is in that sense "subjective" rather than being directed at deciding what would have been beyond the control of an abstract or "reasonable" person. A second point is that what is "beyond control" should be tested by considering whether the happening of the event was or was not within the control of the applicant in a practical or realistic sense.

2411742 (Refugee)

27 Aug 2024Administrative Review Tribunal[2024] AATA 4375Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa refusal reviewVisa integrityMigration
Before: Damian Creedon
The applicant is an older South Korean citizen who claimed protection in Australia because he feared being unable to find work in South Korea due to age discrimination and long absence. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal of his protection visa, finding South Korea offers effective protection against age discrimination and that his economic/employment concerns did not meet protection criteria.
Key holding

Effective protection measures available from the receiving State can negate a well-founded fear of persecution under s 5J(2).

The Tribunal finds, therefore, that South Korea can offer effective protection to its citizens against age discrimination. It follows, and the Tribunal finds, that effective protection measures against age discrimination are available to the applicant in South Korea, and that therefore he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution on that ground: s 5J(2).

Adam v Secretary of Department of Home Affairs

28 Feb 2024Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia[2024] FedCFamC2G 179Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationMigration
The applicant, an Iranian-born refugee, sought a writ of habeas corpus after spending 2.5 years in immigration detention without being removed to Iran. The Court found that, absent a valid travel document and given Iran's refusal to accept involuntary returnees, there was no real prospect of his removal becoming practicable in the reasonably foreseeable future, so his continued detention exceeded the constitutional limit.

The Court found that a fair-minded lay observer might apprehend bias and granted writs of prohibition, certiorari, and mandamus, quashing the Tribunal's decision and requiring it to redetermine the matter according to law.

March 2001 (1)

Re Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs; Ex parte Cohen

1 Mar 2001High Court of Australia[2001] HCA 10Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewMigration
Meir Cohen sought constitutional relief in the High Court alleging the Migration Review Tribunal committed jurisdictional error by applying an erroneous precedent (Huang) in interpreting 'disability' and 'other serious circumstance' in the 'special need relative' definition in reg 1.03. McHugh J held that applying an incorrect interpretation of non-technical factual expressions, even via an erroneous precedent, did not amount to jurisdictional error, and that the writs sought against the Minister and Principal Member were misconceived.

The prosecutor, an Ethiopian asylum seeker detained at Villawood, sought prerogative relief in the High Court under s75(v) of the Constitution following dismissal of her Federal Court judicial review of a Refugee Review Tribunal decision refusing her protection visa.
